title: Window and Door Rebates in Fort St. John 2026: $100 Each, Up to $2,000
desc: Fort St. John has the coldest winters in our BC list. BC Hydro pays $100 per window or door, up to $2,000. Rules, a worked example and steps.
h1: Window and Door Rebates in Fort St. John
lead: Fort St. John's January low averages -15.0°C, the coldest in our BC list. A window with a low U-factor matters more here than anywhere else we cover.
cards_heading: What BC Hydro pays for windows and doors in Fort St. John
cards_intro: We re-read BC Hydro's window and door page on October 2, 2026. The rebate is for homes heated mainly by electricity. FortisBC lists $100 per opening for its gas customers, except in the City of Vancouver.

cards.title: Windows and doors
cards.note: Paid for each window or door that replaces an existing one between a heated space and outdoors.

cards.title: Cap
cards.note: That is 20 openings at $100 each. A bay window counts as one opening.

cards.title: Energy rating
cards.note: The window or door must have a maximum U-factor of 1.22 W/m2-K, which is BC Hydro's Tier 2 level.

cards.title: More than one upgrade
cards.note: BC Hydro adds a bonus when you finish more than one eligible upgrade.

cards.title: Lower incomes
cards.note: Income-qualified customers can apply for free upgrades.

after_cards:
A Fort St. John 1970s bungalow

A bungalow with 10 windows, a front door and a side door is 12 openings. That pays $1,200. In a climate this cold, the real gain is less draft and fewer cold spots near the glass.
sections: Fort St. John's homes in numbers

The 2021 Census counted 8,775 households in Fort St. John. About 3,690 (42%) live in homes built before 1981, and 2,035 are owner-occupied detached houses from that period. Half live in detached houses and 42% rent. About 7.5% say their home needs major repairs, the highest share in our BC list.

Fort St. John's average January low from 2015 to 2024 was -15.0°C and the coldest day was -42.2°C. That is about 5 degrees colder than Prince George on average. Cold glass pulls heat from the room, so the area around old windows feels cold even with the heat on.

The home must be mainly electric-heated and at least 12 months old. A natural gas, oil or propane home is not eligible for BC Hydro's version. The BC Hydro account holder applies, or signs a consent form for someone else to apply, which matters in a city where 42% of households rent.

Each rough opening counts as one. A bay window is one. Skylights are excluded. Units need a U-factor of 1.22 W/m2-K or lower and a listing from CSA, Intertek, Labtest, QAI or NFRC. In a cold climate, ask for the lowest U-factor in your budget, since 1.22 is the minimum, not the best available.

The rebate needs a U-factor of 1.22 W/m2-K or lower, and lower means less heat loss. Many window labels show the older imperial scale instead. To convert, multiply the imperial number by 5.678. A label that says U-0.30 equals 1.70 W/m2-K, which is too high. A label that says U-0.21 equals about 1.19 W/m2-K and passes. Ask the contractor to quote the metric value for each model so you do not have to convert.

BC Hydro pays a bonus of up to $2,000 when you finish more than one eligible upgrade, but its page does not give a formula, so ask when you apply. FortisBC lists a $300 second-upgrade bonus or an EnerGuide improvement bonus of $750 to $2,000. Windows pair naturally with insulation, since both cut heat loss through the building envelope.

BC Hydro sends income-qualified customers to the CleanBC Better Homes Energy Savings Program instead, and the two cannot be combined. The 2026 program document lists no insulation or window rebates, so the free Energy Conservation Assistance Program is the route to ask about.
claim_heading: How to claim in Fort St. John
claim_steps: Check the home is electric-heated and at least 12 months old.
Get quotes that list the U-factor of each unit.
Photograph each label on installation day.
Keep the invoice and apply within six months.
Add insulation to the same application to check the bonus.
